Urdu BPE Tokenizer from Scratch
1. Overview
This report describes the byte-level BPE tokenizer we built for Urdu without using any tokenizer library. We collected and
cleaned a multi-genre corpus (over 600 MB raw), wrote the Unicode normaliser and the tokenizer ourselves, trained a
vocabulary of exactly 50,000 tokens, and then compared it with GPT-2 and o200k_base on held-out text. Sections 3 to 5
answer the three analysis questions of Part C, and Section 6 lists what we are submitting and how to rebuild it.
Design choice
What we did
Base vocabulary
IDs 0–255 are the raw byte values, so every string can be encoded and decoded without loss and there is
never an unknown token.
Special token
<|endoftext|> has ID 256 and is kept out of every merge.
Merges
49,743 merges, IDs 257 to 49,999, stored in the order they were learned.
Tie-breaking
When two pairs have the same count we merge the lexicographically greater pair (id1, id2), which makes
training deterministic.
Pre-tokenisation
A custom regex (regex module) that keeps combining marks (\p{M}) and ZWNJ (U+200C) inside the
word, so diacritics do not split Urdu words the way GPT-2’s pattern does. A leading space stays attached to
the following word.
Training
Two stages. A reference version recounts every pair after each merge and was used for checking. The fast
version counts each distinct word once, keeps a pair-to-words index so only affected words are updated,
and caches word encodings. The fast version was used for the full run.
Normalisation
Done in normalize.py, outside the tokenizer, and idempotent (normalising twice gives the same text).
Table 1. Main design decisions.

3. Question 1: What Did the Merges Learn?
Every letter in the Arabic-script block (U+0600–U+06FF) takes two bytes in UTF-8: a lead byte between 0xD8 and 0xDB
and a continuation byte. Before the tokenizer can learn anything word-like, it has to glue these byte pairs back into letters.

Table 6. The token created at every 5,000th merge.
Merges 3 and 5 are not letters: they join a space with the lead byte of the next letter (0xD8 or 0xD9). That is why they are
not valid UTF-8 on their own. In total 114 of the 49,743 merged tokens are not valid UTF-8 when decoded alone (examples
in Table 7). They are by-products of building letters and punctuation out of bytes, and they act as bridges that let later merges
create space-prefixed words in one step. Merge 12, for instance, is alif plus the lead byte of the next letter, merge 38 adds a
space in front of it, and merge 100 is 0xE2 0x80, the first two bytes of three-byte punctuation such as curly quotes and dashes.
The first whole word is  (“of”) at merge 28 (ID 284), stored together with its leading space. Next come  at merge 29,
 at merge 40,  at merge 46 and  at merge 48, so within the first 50 merges the vocabulary already contains the most
common Urdu function words. Table 6 shows the general trend after that: short words and function words early, whole nouns
by merge 5,000, names and longer words between 15,000 and 30,000, and a mix of punctuation, inflected forms and English
words after 40,000.

The longest tokens are not words at all. Ranks 1 to 4 are runs of the Urdu full stop or of hyphens, decorative separator lines
that appear in scraped pages, rank 5 is a run of kasratan marks, and ranks 6 and 7 are heavily vowelled Arabic phrases that
look like quotations from religious text. Figure 1 shows the overall picture: token length starts at two bytes and then settles
at an average of roughly 8 to 12 bytes.

4. Question 2: Comparison with Existing Tokenizers
We compared our tokenizer with GPT-2 (gpt2, 50,257 tokens) and OpenAI’s multilingual o200k_base (200,000 tokens),
using tiktoken for the two reference encodings only. The held-out test split has 1,952 documents, 3,112,488 characters and
649,343 words (5.23 MB of text).

On the test split our tokenizer needs 1.155 tokens per word, against 6.05 for GPT-2, so sequences are about 5.2 times shorter
(81% fewer tokens). It also produces 27.8% fewer tokens than o200k_base with a quarter of its vocabulary. This comparison
is not entirely fair, though: our merges were learned on text from the same sources as the test split, while o200k_base is a
general multilingual tokenizer. The numbers show how well the vocabulary fits Urdu text of this kind, not a general ranking.

News, poetry and personal names stay between 1.04 and 1.15 tokens per word, and Urdu mixed with English costs a little
more at 1.31. Fully vowelled text is the hardest case for us (3.57), although the other two tokenizers do worse on it. The one
place where we lose is Roman Urdu: 2.64 tokens per word against 1.68 for o200k_base and 2.11 for GPT-2. That is what
we expected, since the whole corpus is in Perso-Arabic script.
5. Question 3: Inputs the Tokenizer Handles Badly
Case 1: Roman Urdu with stretched letters
“yrrr plzzzzz mujhy btao ye assignment kb tk submit krwani h wrna scene off hojana”
15 words. Ours: 42 tokens (2.80 per word) o200k_base: 25 GPT-2: 29. Our split: yr | r | r | pl | z | z | z | z | z | m | uj | hy …
Our corpus is entirely Perso-Arabic script, so the vocabulary has almost no merges for Latin letter combinations. Informal
chat spelling with repeated letters (“yrrr”, “plzzzzz”) therefore falls back to single ASCII bytes, and the result is worse than
both reference tokenizers.

6 words. Ours: 39 tokens (6.50 per word) o200k_base: 49 GPT-2: 77.
Our pattern keeps combining marks attached to their word, so they are not cut off during pre-tokenisation, but BPE can only
merge combinations it saw often. Most modern Urdu is written without short-vowel marks, so letter-plus-mark combinations
rarely reached the frequency needed. Nearly every mark ends up as its own two-byte token, which gives 6.5 tokens per word
compared with about 1.1 on ordinary prose.

4
Case 3: Honorific signs and rare ligatures

12 words. Ours: 12 tokens o200k_base: 22 GPT-2: 59.
This sentence is handled well, and common words become single tokens, but it shows where the weak spot is. The honorific
ligature ﷺ (U+FDFA) is a single code point that takes three bytes, and the signs ؓ (U+0613) and ؑ (U+0611) take two bytes
each. Rarer ligatures such as ﷽ (U+FDFD) are not frequent enough to earn merges; in our tests they fell back to byte pieces.
A corpus with more religious text, or an explicit step that keeps these symbols whole, would help.
6. Deliverables and Reproduction
The archive contains normalize.py (normaliser), bpe.py (the BPETokenizer class with the reference and fast trainers),
train_tokenizer.py (training runner that also records the hardware details), encode_corpus.py (streaming encoder
with a word cache that writes the uint16 files), tokenizer.json (vocabulary and all 49,743 merges), DATA_CARD.md,
README.md and this report. The text corpus and the binary files are on the shared drive (links on the cover page). To rebuild
everything from train.txt:
# 1. unit tests
python tests/test_normalize.py
python tests/test_bpe.py
# 2. train the 50,000-token vocabulary
python train_tokenizer.py --input corpus/train.txt --vocab-size 50000 --output tokenizer.json
# 3. encode the corpus to flat uint16 arrays
python encode_corpus.py --tokenizer tokenizer.json --train-in corpus/train.txt \
--val-in corpus/val.txt --train-out data/train.bin --val-out data/val.bin
# 4. regenerate the Part C analysis
python scripts/analyze_tokenizer.py
